paragraphs: Here's what I love about this passage, friend. Nobody in Israel was told to light the lamps once and call it a day. The LORD says the lamps are to burn "continually," and the bread is to be set out before Him "every Sabbath day" (Leviticus 24:2, 8). Worship in this place was not a big moment once in a while. It was steady, daily, and it did not stop.

Now look at who does the work. Israelites bring the oil, Aaron tends the lamps, and twelve loaves go on a table of pure gold. Everyone has a part, and the LORD set it up that way. The bread is set out "on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant," and it is "a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD," which Aaron and his sons eat in a holy place (Leviticus 24:8, 9). The LORD cared about the details of how He was approached, and He still does.

So here's what I'd carry out of my bakery today, baker. Showing up with the same small faithful thing again and again matters to God. Not just on the big days, but on the ordinary evenings, when it feels like nobody is watching. The lamps just kept burning, and that was the whole point. And I'll tell you what, after my years in that drawer, I know a light that stays on is a gift. The LORD isn't done teaching His people about being holy, so keep that oven warm.
